answer.rationale: The mandate (18% cut) plus the incumbent's refusal to reopen price effectively closes negotiate_terms and renew_incumbent as standalone answers, and defer_decision is unsafe because the contract does not auto-renew and lapses in 14 days. That leaves the low-cost vendor. The single memory carrying the most weight for that move is memory_c2 (cheap, fast onboarding, clean invoicing), so it is the one I most need to see in original form: I need to know whether it describes a component of comparable criticality, what the utilization headroom was during that ramp, and whether 'quick onboarding' meant qualified-and-at-volume or merely contracted. A cost win recorded on a slack line does not transfer to a line at 94% of committed volume with no buffer. I also verify memory_c3, because the second-source lesson is the natural risk hedge here and I need to know whether it was a true dual-award with allocation guarantees or an opportunistic backup; if the former, the right structure is a majority tranche to the low-cost vendor with the incumbent retained on a bridge for the balance rather than a clean cutover. Hence standard_experiment rather than broad_rollout: shift a defined volume tranche with qualification gates and a fallback, not the whole line. Downstream risk is real and flagged: every one of these memories records an outcome under conditions I cannot see, and the consolidated summaries have already stripped the failure modes; if the archive contradicts memory_c2's applicability, I fall back to a short bridge with the incumbent on non-price terms and re-decide next review. Delivery continuity is the binding constraint, not the cost target, and I will not trade the line for the 18%.
